This chain does not contain all of Ezra's forefathers, but the most important of them were chosen; fifteen persons are mentioned here, but the complete chain contains 30 priests.

Ezra was a priest and not a high priest, but he was a scribe who cared about copying the Law of God, so he understood it and was able to explain its meanings. The scribes were few, and therefore they were highly esteemed; that is, Ezra had a great standing as a spiritual leader, in addition to his being the leader of the second company of those returning to Jerusalem.

Ezra the priest did not practice his priestly work, because he lived in Babylon, and God blessed him, so he obtained the position of a scribe in the court of the Persian king Artaxerxes, which was an important position.
In addition to this, Ezra took care to write the Law and was skilled, not only in writing it but also in understanding the Law, so that he was able to be an expounder of it to the Jews around him.
But how did the Law of Moses reach Babylon? There are many possibilities, among them:
1- The captives carried it from Jerusalem to Babylon when they were taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar.

2- When Nebuchadnezzar seized the vessels of the house of the Lord and everything in it, he may have found among them the book of the Law and carried it with the vessels, and Ezra discovered it afterward, because he worked in the royal court, so he cared for this copy and began to copy from it, read it and understand it.

Since God saw Ezra's heart that loved Him, his care for the Law and the worship of the Lord, and his longing to practice his priestly service in Jerusalem, He blessed him, helped him and gave him the desire of his heart, making his return to Jerusalem easy for him, and King Artaxerxes agreed to this and encouraged him with many reinforcements. We feel the blessing of God with Ezra in the repetition of the phrase "the hand of the Lord upon Ezra", which is mentioned six times in (chs. 7, 8), and this means God's love and obedience and Ezra's love for His commandments.

The Nethinim: They were Gentiles from Gibeon who joined the people of God in the days of Joshua, and he made them drawers of water and hewers of wood for the service of the temple. They loved the God of Israel, so they returned from captivity to serve His house. A great number of Jews went up with Ezra to Jerusalem from Babylon, nearly eight thousand, and they were from the different classes of the people; some were priests and others were servants of the temple, such as the Levites, the singers, the porters and the Nethinim.

The return of Ezra and those with him to Jerusalem was in the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and this king loved the Jews, so Ezra returned in his days, and thirteen years after him Nehemiah returned by order of the same king.

The return of the Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem took place in three stages: the first under Zerubbabel, the second under Ezra and the third under Nehemiah, so that God would give an opportunity to everyone who loves Him and loves His house to return to Jerusalem. God wants everyone to return and encourages them, so whoever could not return with the first company has an opportunity with the second or the third. We see the hand of God that encouraged the kings Cyrus and Artaxerxes and prepared the hearts of His children Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, in order to encourage as many as possible to return to Him. But the people's response was weak because of their attachment to the material things of the world. They loved the world more than God and remained in captivity, enduring bondage for the sake of worldly possessions and lusts.

The caravan moved under the leadership of Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem; it set out in the first month and arrived at the beginning of the fifth month, that is, the journey took four months, in which the faith of Ezra and the Jews and their reliance on God appeared, because they did not ask the king for a guard. On the other hand, the care of God and His preservation of His children appeared, until they arrived in peace at the holy city of Jerusalem. The distance they covered on this journey was about 900 miles.
Statute: worship and rites.
Judgments: rulings, that is, commandments and laws.

Ezra took care to read the Law, understand it and meditate on its meanings, so his heart clung to it. After this he practiced this Law in his life and held to it with all exactness, so the Jews saw him and learned from him the keeping of the Law. Then Ezra was able to teach the people the Law, and they received it easily from him, because they had seen it first in him, and God blessed him greatly for his faithfulness in these three stages: keeping, practicing and then teaching. What is beautiful in Ezra is that he cared for the Law, kept it and practiced it in Babylon, far from the house of the Lord. He loved God although he was surrounded by pagans, so when he arrived in Jerusalem he was encouraged and was very distinguished in practicing the Law and teaching it.

Take care to read the Bible every day and meditate on it, so that you can apply it in your life as a personal message to you in your life, and then you can be a light to the world and teach the word of God, and people will accept it from you.

King Artaxerxes supported Ezra the scribe, who worked for him, with a royal letter containing great orders for the care of the house of the Lord, in which the strong hand of God appears, which moved the king to support Ezra and those returning with him from captivity.

Artaxerxes styles himself king of kings, because he was an emperor who reigned over 127 provinces, among them the province of the Jews (Esth 1:1). This means that he was the greatest man in the world at that time, since he ruled the largest number of lands. He styles Ezra a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, perfect peace, so he is not merely a scribe for the king but in addition he is the scribe of the law of God. This shows his esteem for Ezra. He styles God the God of heaven, the perfect, and this shows his esteem for God, for in his view He is not a god like the rest of the gods, but distinguished in that He is the God of heaven and that He is perfect. His esteem for God gives greater standing to His scribe, who is Ezra, and this is the first time a pagan king has styled God perfect.

Ezra was the chief of the scribes of the Law. He began his work in captivity and continued afterward in Jerusalem, and remained a scribe for eighty years, and he was distinguished by being both a scribe and a priest.

It appears in these two verses that Artaxerxes is the one who sent Ezra to inquire about and care for the Jews, and it was not Ezra who asked the king, as happened in the case of Nehemiah. This was of course by the providence of God, who moved the king to love the God of the Jews and call Him the God of heaven, the perfect, and to ask the blessing of this God and care for the welfare of His people who believe in Him.

The order issued is from the king and his seven counselors, and this was a system known among the Persians, which we also see with Ahasuerus the father of Artaxerxes (Esth 1:14). The number seven was honored among the Gentiles. These counselors were heads of fathers in Persia and represented a council that issued the royal orders under the leadership of the king, for it was the highest council in the empire and the ruling council.

Ezra was commissioned with authority from the king to care for the Jews, and at the same time he carried out the Law of God with all its reward and punishment, for by the authority of the king he executes and judges by the Law. This shows the king's trust in Ezra in addition to his trust in the Law of God.

The Jews could not have imagined a better situation than this for the application of the commandments and laws of God. Consequently Ezra had the right to appoint judges and governors under him to carry out the Law of God, supported by the order of the emperor Artaxerxes.

By the king's choosing Ezra and commanding him to apply the Law of God, he was able to win the Jews and secure their loyalty to him, since they would be ruled by one of their own and by the law of their God, a distinguished and wise man, a priest and scribe who understood the Law of God.

God commanded Ezra to take with him whoever wished of the priests, the Levites and the people to return with him to Jerusalem, and in this he supports the service of the house of the Lord and its worship and shows his love for the Jews.

After Artaxerxes commanded Ezra to visit and care for the Jews in Jerusalem and to make sure of their adherence to the Law of God, this is the first item of the order of Artaxerxes, which is mentioned in (vv. 13, 14). The second item is that Ezra should take with him the gold and silver that the king and his seven counselors had freely offered to the house of the Lord which is in Jerusalem. This means the esteem, respect and faith of Artaxerxes and his counselors in God and their submission to Him as a great God. The wonder appears here in the submission of the chiefs of the Gentiles to God and their honoring of His house at the time when the Jews and their kings neglected the care of the house of the Lord, as happened before the captivity.

The third item in the king's order is the collection of contributions of silver and gold from the Gentile inhabitants of the land of Babylon, in addition to what he collects from the Jews in captivity in the land of Babylon, whether priests, Levites or the rest of the Jews. Here the king's concern appears that all his people should submit and care for the house of the Lord and revere God. The wonder is that he alerts the Jews who remained in captivity out of attachment to their possessions and whose hearts were not moved to go and worship their God in Jerusalem, or at least to contribute to the house of the Lord; for if Artaxerxes had been a Jew he would not have said more than this for the care of the house of the Lord.

May you be ashamed when you see the reverence of some unbelievers for your Church, your Christ and your saints, so that your heart may be moved, you may live for God, be committed to your worship and honor the saints.

The fourth item in the order of Artaxerxes is the purchase of livestock with the silver and gold to be offered as sacrifices to God in His temple at Jerusalem, in addition to the rest of the offerings and drink offerings of wine. The fifth item in the king's order is giving Ezra freedom to buy with the rest of the silver and gold whatever he sees that the temple needs, for the king wants the worship in the temple to go on in the best way. We notice here the following:
1- Giving Ezra freedom as he sees the service to need, so that he may arrange it with all care.

2- The king's concern for consultation among the leaders of the Jews for the arrangement of the service of the temple, because the king himself follows consultation in leading the kingdom of Persia, as he had seven counselors.
3- The king's concern for the Law of God and His will, so he asks Ezra that they do everything in accordance with the will of God, that they may gain His satisfaction.

The king's concern to honor God appears in his offering precious vessels of silver and gold, or any other valuable materials, in addition to the vessels that the Jews and the Gentiles contributed to the house of the Lord. All this Ezra hands over to those responsible for the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, to be at their disposal for carrying out the service of the house of the Lord.
These vessels are not the vessels of the house of the Lord that returned with Zerubbabel, but precious vessels that were contributed to the house of the Lord.

The sixth item in the king's order is that Ezra may draw what he needs of money, in addition to the service of the house of the Lord, from the king's treasuries in the region beyond the river, and the king issued an order to those in charge of these treasuries to give Ezra what he asks of money and also what he asks of wheat, wine, oil and salt in large quantities as he needs, even if it reaches:
1- A hundred talents of silver, equal to about 3,000 kilograms.
2- A hundred cors of wheat, equal to about 150,000 kilograms.
3- A hundred baths of wine, oil and salt, equal to 2,300 liters.

We see the king's concern in his order to the treasurers to give quickly all that Ezra asks, for he is concerned to provide the service of the house of the Lord as quickly as possible, and this is great love and esteem for God.
We see in this verse the following:
1- The king's feeling that all he does is by the commands of God, that is, that the king is an instrument in the hand of God carrying out His will, which is a living, practical faith in God.
2- The fear of God in the king's heart, for he wants to please God so that He will not be angry with him.

It is strange that the people of God did evil in the eyes of God, so captivity fell upon them, while the pagan king fears God and carries out His orders exactly. And after the return from captivity the Jews bound themselves in pagan marriages, contrary to the Law of God, while the pagan king in Babylon submits to the orders of God and fears Him. It should have been the opposite, because the people of God dwell in Jerusalem where the temple is, and the worship of God and the fear of Him should have influenced them more than the king.
At this time a rebellion took place in Egypt, so Artaxerxes sent soldiers to subdue it, and he wanted God's satisfaction with him so as to establish his kingdom and his sons' after him.

The seventh item in the king's order is the lifting of taxes from the priests and the servants of the temple, because they are consecrated to the service of the house of the Lord so that they might devote themselves to His service without care or other financial responsibilities, and this is of course a great honor to God, His house and His servants.

The eighth item in the order of Artaxerxes is that Ezra should choose rulers and judges from the Jews who know the Law of God, so that they may teach the people how to worship God and please Him in all their life. He also commanded him to take care to teach the rulers and judges, that they might complete their knowledge of the Law of God. Ezra is the head responsible for the learning of the people, so he teaches a group, the rulers and judges, with all exactness, so that they may teach the rest of the people.

Here we see the king walking in the thought of the New Testament, which the Didascalia expresses: "Wipe out iniquity by teaching", so he cares for teaching the people before punishing them when they sin, and the king directs Ezra to walk in this thought.

The ninth and last item in the king's order is the severe punishment of every Jew who violates the Law of God, according to the kind of his violation, either by death, or banishment to a far place where he suffers loneliness, or imprisonment, or payment of a fine.

From this we understand that Ezra was a religious leader who had the right to punish whoever violated the Law, but he was not a governor responsible for civil offenses, or for non-Jews. From the order of King Artaxerxes to Ezra we see his great trust in him, which shows us many qualities that were all gathered in his person, namely:
1- The king commanded Ezra to inquire about those returning from captivity, out of trust in his fatherly care (v. 14).
2- He gave him the silver and gold, confident of his faithfulness (vv. 15, 16).
3- He granted him freedom to dispose of the silver and gold, confident of his wisdom (v. 18).
4- He gave him the authority to take what he needed of money and foodstuffs from the king's treasuries in the region beyond the river, out of trust in his contentment (vv. 20, 21).
5- He charged him with appointing rulers and judges to guide the people, confident of his good administration (v. 25).
6- He asked him to take care to teach these rulers and judges and all the people, confident of his knowledge and his ability to teach (v. 25).
7- He also gave him the authority to punish offenders with the various punishments, confident of his justice (v. 26).

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: When Ezra received this great letter from Artaxerxes he felt that he was before divine gifts he had never imagined, so he praised God, saying "Blessed be the LORD God of our fathers", remembering the love of God, who fulfills His covenants to the fathers, so He forgives His people despite the multitude of their sins when they repent, and gathers them from the dispersion of the world to worship Him in His temple at Jerusalem.

Ezra did not build the house of the Lord but he beautified it, not with drawings and ornaments but by organizing the service of the priests and Levites, teaching them with the people the Law of God, and his care for the continuation of the service with all exactness every day before the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ezra thanked God for the grace He gave him in the eyes of the king and the great divine mercy in the king's order to him to return with the Jews to Jerusalem. Ezra had not asked the king, but it was the king who commanded him to do this, and of course that was because God moved the king's heart.

Ezra did not ascribe the work and the glory to himself in the return to Jerusalem, but ascribed it to the hand of God working in the king and in him, and he is truly a great man because of his great humility.

We also notice Ezra's energy and enthusiasm in seizing this opportunity, that is, the king's order, so he strengthened himself and gathered those of the Jews who wished to return and led them, with all the gifts he was able to gather, to Jerusalem.

How beautiful it is to thank God for His daily blessings to you! He is a tender Father always caring for you, and His gifts toward you never cease if you are spiritually watchful, so become accustomed to thanksgiving until your inner eyes are enlightened and you discover His providence and care for you.
The second return to Jerusalem under Ezra

1- We notice in the return of the Jews to Jerusalem that none of the kings, Cyrus or Artaxerxes, commanded that all the Jews be compelled to return, because God respects man's freedom and waits for man to choose by himself to return to God.

2- The return was in three groups to show the extent of the response of the people and the priests, for some hastened with Zerubbabel and others after a period, then the last were with Nehemiah, as Christ mentioned in the parable of the laborers, some at the first hour and others in successive hours until the eleventh hour.

3- The leaders were different: Zerubbabel was of royal descent, Ezra was of the priests, and Nehemiah was of the people and obtained a position in Persian society, for God accepts all in His service with the variety of their abilities.
4- Each company that returned to Jerusalem had a role:
a - The first company built the temple.
b - The second company organized the service in the temple.
c - The third company built the walls of Jerusalem and its gates.
Thus the roles of the companies were complementary in working for the good of the people and their relationship with God, and all took care of inward reform.
5- The hand of God appears in this chapter, accompanying His people and preserving them until they reached Jerusalem from the land of Babylon, so that they might begin to thank God and worship Him.

6- With the end of the previous chapter the writing in the Aramaic language ends, because the preceding chapters contain royal letters, and from this chapter Ezra begins to write in the Hebrew language, because he addresses the Jewish people, who are fluent in Hebrew.
(1) The heads of the fathers who returned (vv. 1-14)
1- These are now the chief of their fathers, and this is the genealogy of them that went up with me from Babylon, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king.

2- Of the sons of Phinehas; Gershom: of the sons of Ithamar; Daniel: of the sons of David; Hattush. 3- Of the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh; Zechariah: and with him were reckoned by genealogy of the males an hundred and fifty. 4- Of the sons of Pahathmoab; Elihoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males. 5- Of the sons of Shechaniah; the son of Jahaziel, and with him three hundred males. 6- Of the sons also of Adin; Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him fifty males. 7- And of the sons of Elam; Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him seventy males. 8- And of the sons of Shephatiah; Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him fourscore males. 9- Of the sons of Joab; Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him two hundred and eighteen males. 10- And of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah, and with him an hundred and threescore males. 11- And of the sons of Bebai; Zechariah the son of Bebai, and with him twenty and eight males.

12- And of the sons of Azgad; Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him an hundred and ten males. 13- And of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males. 14- Of the sons also of Bigvai; Uthai, and Zabbud, and with them seventy males.

1- At the end of the previous chapter Ezra tells us of his return with those of the Jews who accepted to return to Jerusalem. In this verse he tells us of the heads of the fathers returning to Jerusalem and mentions their details in the following verses.

2- Ezra's concern was to write down the heads of the fathers, because each head would bring those who followed him from his clan, and so he mentions to us a large group of clans from which people returned.

3- If we add up the numbers of those returning mentioned in these verses, we find 1,496, to which is added an unknown number referred to in (v. 2), so the estimated number of the men returning was about 1,700 men. If we add to them the women and children, the number is about eight thousand.
4- The returning priests are mentioned at the beginning (v. 2) because of their importance in the service of the house of the Lord.

5- It is mentioned in (v. 13) "the last sons of Adonikam" because a large number of his sons returned with Zerubbabel, and here we find 60 other men returning with Ezra, so it is understood from this that from the same clans a part returned in the first company and some in the second company.

God rejoices at your returning to Him, even if you have delayed in returning and been hindered, and did not go up with Zerubbabel. Now you have an opportunity to return with Ezra, that is, to return to Him with repentance and spiritual zeal to hold fast to His commandments and spiritual practices.
(2) The preparation for the return (vv. 15-30)

15- And I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days: and I viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi. 16- Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding. 17- And I sent them with commandment unto Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia, and I told them what they should say unto Iddo, and to his brethren the Nethinims, at the place Casiphia, that they should bring unto us ministers for the house of our God. 18- And by the good hand of our God upon us they brought us a man of understanding, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel; and Sherebiah, with his sons and his brethren, eighteen; 19- And Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brethren and their sons, twenty; 20- Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name. 21- Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance. 22- For I was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy in the way: because we had spoken unto the king, saying, The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him; but his power and his wrath is against all them that forsake him. 23- So we fasted and besought our God for this: and he was intreated of us. 24- Then I separated twelve of the chief of the priests, Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brethren with them, 25- And weighed unto them the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, even the offering of the house of our God, which the king, and his counsellors, and his lords, and all Israel there present, had offered: 26- I even weighed unto their hand six hundred and fifty talents of silver, and silver vessels an hundred talents, and of gold an hundred talents; 27- Also twenty basons of gold, of a thousand drams; and two vessels of fine copper, precious as gold. 28- And I said unto them, Ye are holy unto the LORD; the vessels are holy also; and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering unto the LORD God of your fathers. 29- Watch ye, and keep them, until ye weigh them before the chief of the priests and the Levites, and chief of the fathers of Israel, at Jerusalem, in the chambers of the house of the LORD. 30- So took the priests and the Levites the weight of the silver, and the gold, and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem unto the house of our God.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ahava: one of the tributaries of the Euphrates near Babylon, where there was a gathering of the Jews, since they preferred to live beside rivers so that it would be easy for them to wash when offering their worship to God, as the Psalm says, "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down" (Ps 137:1), and Ezekiel also lived in captivity beside the Chebar (Ezek 1:1). Casiphia: a word meaning silver, and it is a region in Media with silver mines, around which the Levites gathered; perhaps they worked in these mines.

1- Ezra gathered those who wished to return from captivity at the river Ahava, and perhaps he organized them and learned their genealogies, mentioned in (vv. 1-14), and that was during three days. He discovered the presence of a number of priests and people but found none of the Levites.

2- The gathering of the people for three days at the river is a type of the Resurrection of Christ, whose power we receive through the sacrament of Baptism and the work of the Holy Spirit in it, which the water signifies.

3- Ezra was not content to grieve over the Levites' lack of response, but chose ten of his assistants and sent them under the leadership of two men whom he called men of understanding. All ten were heads of fathers, but two of them were distinguished by understanding and the ability to speak and persuade (v. 16). He sent these to a man named Iddo who lived in the region of Casiphia, which, as we mentioned, probably had living in it a number of Levites and Nethinim, that is, the Gentiles who helped in the service of the temple. Iddo is styled the chief, and perhaps he was the head of a school of the Levites.

4- Ezra's assistants were able to persuade Iddo to call among the Levites and the Nethinim to return to Jerusalem, and Iddo responded, so forty of the Levites were persuaded and went to the river Ahava where Ezra was staying. As for the Nethinim, a large number of them responded, 220, and they too went to Ezra. This shows the extent of the Gentiles' response and the slackness of the Levites who were consecrated to the service of the house of God, for they loved the world and clung to their possessions, so most of them refused to return to Jerusalem. Unfortunately the Levites had already been slack about returning in the days of Zerubbabel, for only 74 Levites returned, and the reasons for that were mentioned previously in (ch. 2:40).
5- We see Ezra's faith and humility in ascribing every blessing in the return to Jerusalem to the hand of God, for he says "according to the good hand of my God upon me" (v. 18).

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: After the people gathered around Ezra at the river Ahava, he proclaimed among them a communal fast, that they might cut off from themselves their material attachments to the land of captivity, for fasting is detachment and leaving the world in order to enjoy God, and by this they can overcome the wars of the devil, as Christ said, "this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting" (Mt 17:21). And if they gathered at the river Ahava, which signifies Baptism, they need, after receiving the new nature, to keep it by means of fasting, which attaches their hearts to the love of God and not the world. This is the greatest preparation for the spiritual journey, that is, returning to God, for returning to God requires weaning from the world. The journey of returning to God also requires repentance, so Ezra proclaimed humbling themselves before God, that He might accept their repentance, so that they would be cleansed from every sin and God would enlighten their eyes and they would walk in the right way and keep His commandments.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: His power: His authority and strength in the war with Satan.

Ezra looked at the length of the return journey, which was about 900 miles, and at the possibility of robbers and enemies, especially since he had with him thousands of women and children, in addition to precious possessions, namely silver, gold and valuable vessels estimated at millions of pounds. In the face of these fears Ezra felt the need for protection and care.

Ezra thought of asking the king for guards to accompany him on the road, but he quickly drew back and was ashamed to ask for that, for how could he believe in a mighty God able to preserve him and ask for human help? So he rejected this thought and believed in God and relied on Him.

If Nehemiah accepted guards to accompany him from the same King Artaxerxes and thanked him for it, this does not mean that Nehemiah's faith was weak, for he too was ashamed to refuse the king's soldiers. Both Ezra and Nehemiah believed in the power of God accompanying them and preserving those with them... God works by all means, and what remains is for us to believe in His work in all circumstances.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ezra felt reassured after he had prayed and fasted with the people and God had answered him, and he began the journey, which took about four months, and arrived in peace at Jerusalem. That is, God answered and preserved His children and those who sought Him from two things:
1- From all the dangers that they might meet on the road.
2- He preserved them in unity, so they did not divide against one another, but walked in unity and in submission to Ezra.

Your God is able to preserve you in the midst of all dangers. He asks only for your love, your prayers, your fasting and your seeking of Him. He wants your heart and promises you complete peace, even if you walk through the valley of the shadow of death.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ezra chose twelve men known for faithfulness and exactness from the chief of the priests; two of them are mentioned, Sherebiah and Hashabiah.

These twelve may all have been chief priests, that is, heads of priestly divisions. Or only some of them may have been chief priests and the rest priests. Sherebiah and Hashabiah may have been the heads of the Levites mentioned in (Neh 12:24), and with them ten of the priests and Levites. In sum, they were twelve of those consecrated to the service of the house of the Lord, of the priests or the Levites.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Basin: a vessel, usually small, like a cup or a glass.
Dram of gold: equal to half a shekel, and the shekel is about 12 grams.
Polished: that is, smooth and shining.

Ezra gathered all the silver and gold and the vessels made of silver, gold and fine copper, weighed them and handed them over to these twelve, that they might carry them and keep them on the way of the journey. This shows his good distribution of responsibilities and his care to protect the precious gifts belonging to God. Consequently, if anything of them were lost, no one would think that Ezra had taken anything of them, or that any one person of the twelve had taken it, because the responsibility was collective, and all were responsible for guarding these gifts.
He specified the weights of the silver and gold and the vessels made of them, and likewise those made of copper, and handed them over to these faithful men.
We notice that these gifts were many because:
1- The Persian kingdom was rich.
2- Artaxerxes loved God, so he and his counselors were generous in their giving.
3- The people gave generously to God out of their love for His house.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ezra declared to the men that they were holy and consecrated to the service of God, and likewise that these vessels were holy to God. The holy man esteems everything that is holy and keeps it until he gives it to God, as he first gave himself to God; that is, the man who has been sanctified is entrusted with holy things. And these holy things are the gifts of the king, his counselors and the people to God, and therefore they became holy and set apart for God, no one can take them, but they are given only to the house of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: Ezra asked Sherebiah and Hashabiah and those with them to keep all that they had received throughout the journey until they reached Jerusalem, and then hand over all they had to the priests and Levites in charge of the treasuries of the house of the Lord. So they took everything from the hand of Ezra and went with it to Jerusalem.

He asked the men to hand over all they had by weight with all exactness, not out of doubt of their faithfulness, but so that no one would doubt them and everything would reach the house of the Lord accurately.
(3) Thanksgiving to God in Jerusalem (vv. 31-36)

31- Then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way. 32- And we came to Jerusalem, and abode there three days. 33- Now on the fourth day was the silver and the gold and the vessels weighed in the house of our God by the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them was Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, Levites;

34- By number and by weight of every one: and all the weight was written at that time. 35- Also the children of those that had been carried away, which were come out of the captivity, offered burnt offerings unto the God of Israel, twelve bullocks for all Israel, ninety and six rams, seventy and seven lambs, twelve he goats for a sin offering: all this was a burnt offering unto the LORD. 36- And they delivered the king's commissions unto the king's lieutenants, and to the governors on this side the river: and they furthered the people, and the house of God.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: After the Jews gathered with Ezra at the river Ahava and fasted, prayed and humbled themselves, the journey set out on the twelfth of the first month, which is the month of Nisan, corresponding to the month of April in the Gregorian year, and arrived at Jerusalem on the first of the fifth month, which is the month of Ab, corresponding to the month of August (ch. 7:9); that is, the journey took about four months.

Ezra did not give us details about the journey to Jerusalem, because this journey signifies our journey in the world until we reach the heavenly Jerusalem. And when we arrive, the period of our life on earth becomes as nothing before the glory of heaven; so also the journey of Ezra, whatever its troubles, is worth nothing compared with their enjoyment of seeing the holy city and the temple of God.

All that Ezra mentions about the journey is that God preserved them from all dangers, whether the enemies, that is, the nations that did not love the Jews, or those who lay in wait by the way, that is, robbers, for the hand of God was caring for them as long as they sought the worship of God and to please Him.

The journey of Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem resembles the journey of Moses from Egypt to the land of Canaan, but the journey of Moses took forty years, while the journey of Ezra was four months. Moses had with him the ark of the covenant of God, the pillar of cloud, the pillar of fire, the rock of water and the manna, but Ezra, who is a second Moses, had with him the hand of God, who preserved them as He preserved the first Moses and his people.

Ezra enjoyed the hand of God that preserved him and his people because he spent three days in prayer, fasting and repentance, and his goal was clear, which was to reach Jerusalem, for God preserves His children and those who seek Him and hold fast to Him.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: After the journey reached Jerusalem, they spent three days there; they did not go to their towns where their fathers had lived in Judea. What did they do in the three days?
1- They thanked God, who had preserved them throughout the journey from all dangers.
2- Perhaps they contemplated the temple which they had long yearned to see and had heard about from their fathers and forefathers.
And of course it is understood that the Jews who had preceded them and settled in Jerusalem welcomed them and hosted them during these three days.
Those returning enjoyed unity, because they began the journey with prayer, fasting and repentance, so they felt their unity within the hand of God on their journey.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: After thanking God for three days, Ezra handed over, through the twelve men whom he had entrusted with the silver, the gold and the vessels, and gave them to the priests and Levites, the servants of the temple and those in charge of the treasury.

We notice the exactness in the handing over of these treasures, for he handed them over by number and by weight, so that his faithfulness and the faithfulness of the men with him would not be doubted, and they wrote down the particulars of what they handed over, to be kept inside the temple for whoever should come after him or deal with these possessions.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: After that they offered sacrifices of thanksgiving to God, who had preserved them on the way and let them enjoy seeing His holy temple.

They offered twelve bullocks for all Israel, and although those returning were from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the Jews after the return from captivity had become one state, even if those returning from the other tribes were very few, because affliction creates unity and love among those who were divided.

They offered burnt offerings to God to declare their inclination to consecrate their hearts to God. And they offered sin offerings, as a declaration of their repentance and their need of God's forgiveness, so their feelings were love and humility.

entries.section: (3) The work of God in the second return

paragraphs.text: The satraps: the civil chiefs among the Persians.

Ezra delivered the orders of King Artaxerxes to the satraps and governors beyond the river, who were responsible for the region where the Jews lived, and they carried out the royal orders at once and supported the Jews with the financial needs from the royal treasuries, and also their needs of foodstuffs. Thus by the grace of God hearts that were hostile to the Jews were changed into hearts that help and support the Jews.

If you live by faith and rely on God, He is able to turn whoever is hostile to you, or does you wrong, into a person who cooperates with you and helps you, so that you may be reassured and grow in your love for God and thank Him at all times.
The prayer of Ezra
When Ezra heard of the spread of foreign marriages among his people, he was deeply affected, and sorrow filled his heart, so he did the following:

1- I rent my garment and my mantle: that is, he tore all his clothes, and this is an old custom in the countries of the East and still continues to this day in some parts of Upper Egypt, as an expression of his not enduring the distress and having no appearance to boast of, but expressing his torn heart by torn outer garments.

The Bible tells us of many who tore their clothes in difficult situations, such as Reuben, when he did not find his brother Joseph in the pit (Gen 37:29), and Jacob when he saw Joseph's coat stained with blood (Gen 37:43), and also Jephthah the Gileadite, who vowed to offer as a sacrifice the first who met him after his victory in the war, and found his daughter (Judg 11:35), and also Job when calamities covered him (Job 1:20).
2- And plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard:

Another old custom of the East as an expression of intense grief, for the beard represents dignity and the hair of the head represents a crown, especially among women, as happened with Job when afflictions came upon him (Job 1:20).
3- And sat down astonished:

Because he had the authority to punish the traitors and command them to leave their foreign wives, but at the same time he saw the weakness of his people and that they might not endure this punishment, so they would leave God because of their attachment to their wives and children and join the Gentiles and worship idols. Therefore he expressed his grief within himself and punished no one, but after thirteen years the spiritual condition of the people improved, so Nehemiah was able to command those married to foreign women to separate from their wives, and he even punished them harshly and struck them and plucked off their hair, and they obeyed him.
Ezra's astonishment was increased by how the people had not learned from their fathers who married foreign women, so God allowed them the captivity to discipline them.
He was also astonished at how the people could violate the Law while they lived around the holy temple of God, that is, how they did not fear God.

And finally he was astonished because he knows the longsuffering of God but also knows His justice and that His anger is severe, so how would this people endure the punishment of God if they did not repent?
Ezra remained astonished, not knowing whether to rebuke them, how to rebuke them, and how not to lose them, having compassion on their weakness, for he wanted their salvation by any means.

Here Ezra's fatherhood and his feeling as a servant for his people appear, for he was not content with not sinning himself, but with love humbled himself before God, that God might have mercy on His people, that is, His children.
The people heard of Ezra's humbling of himself because of his knowledge of the presence of pagan marriages among them, and the following happened:

1- One group whose heart was moved and who feared God behaved like Ezra, for they gathered around him praying and humbling themselves before God that He might have mercy on His people and forgive the offenders.
2- Another group of the people was not affected by Ezra's humbling of himself.
3- A third group remained immersed in sin, indulging evil lusts and pagan marriages.

Those who feared God gathered around Ezra and found him humbled and astonished, as we mentioned in the previous verse, and the Bible's repetition of "his sitting astonished" confirms that he continued for a long time in prayer, humbling himself and astonishment.
Ezra continued in his humbling of himself until the evening and was probably fasting, that is, he spent his whole day in fasting, prayer, repentance and supplication before God for his people.

When the time of the evening offering came, Ezra felt hope, so he arose, lifting his heart to God in the form of this burnt offering which is offered in the evening to please God; that is, he arose to propitiate God by his humbling of himself, namely his torn garments and his submission in his prostration and in his prayer, with his hands spread out before God. He felt that he had no refuge but God, so he poured out his prayers, his tears and his astonishment and committed himself to God, asking for His intervention to cleanse his people and deliver them from their sins.

Ezra's prostration and spreading out of his hands in prayer signifies Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane, when He prostrated Himself and prayed with many tears for the sins of His people. Ezra also resembles Moses, who spread out his hands and prayed until his people prevailed over Amalek.

God looks at your closet, waiting for you to prostrate yourself before Him and offer repentance for your sins and supplications for all whom you love, and He answers the tears that are poured out and the soul that is broken before Him.

Ezra, in his fatherhood to the people, felt that he was responsible for their sins, because as a spiritual leader he is responsible to teach his people and warn them of sins. So he offers repentance for his own shortcoming and not only intercession for his sinning people, and he declared his shame and confusion before God because of these sins. This is a prayer of repentance and confession before God, and it carries two meanings:
1- Ezra's confession of the sins of his people, offering repentance on their behalf.
2- Confidence in God's forgiveness.
3- His sense of the holiness of God, before which he is ashamed to stand.
4- His humility, in his looking to the ground and his inability to lift his face toward God.
Ezra also declares, as one of the people, that their sins have risen over their heads, and have grown up to the heavens. This means the following:
1- The spread of sin among the people, even if a number of them had fallen into pagan marriage, there may be others who had fallen by sight, or thought, or any degree of adultery.
2- Sin humbles man, rises over his head and defiles him.
3- Sin provokes God by growing up to the heavens.

4- Sin spread among the people and many fell into it, so it grew up to the heavens. In this they resemble the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose sins rose up to heaven, so they deserved to die by burning (Gen 18:20). This means Ezra's declaration of his confession of the sin because of which they deserve destruction, but he asks for the mercies of God and His forgiveness.
Ezra asks nothing of God, but confesses his sins as a son in shame before the greatness of his Father, who loves him.
Ezra here is a type of Christ, the righteous and holy, who bore the sins of His people, although He had not sinned in anything.
Our kings and our priests: our civil and spiritual leaders.
The kings of the lands: the kings of the empires that enslaved the Jews, such as Assyria and Babylon. Ezra continues his confession and declares two things:
1- The deep rootedness of the sin of association with pagan practices since the days of the fathers.

2- This sin is abominable and deserved a severe punishment, which was captivity and destruction when the fathers committed this sin. Consequently the sin that took place in the days of Ezra deserves the same punishment, which is destruction, bondage and plunder. It is a confession by Ezra that God is merciful and did not punish them according to their sins despite their doing this abominable sin.
From the LORD: the presence of God.
A nail (peg): a piece of wood by which the tent is fixed in the ground.

The sins of the people of God had been abominable for many years, and God was very longsuffering toward them, but He allowed them to be disciplined, and His wrath came upon them, but for a very short time which God likens to a moment, until they repented and returned to Him. The period of captivity is very short and counts for nothing before the mercies of God, which He gives to His people forever in His Kingdom.

And if sin drove the people out of the land that God had given them, God returns and brings them back to it and establishes them in it, as the tent is fixed by the peg in the ground, on condition that they remain holding fast to His commandments, as He establishes those who believe in Him in His Church forever, as long as they hold fast to Him. The moment is the discipline of the captivity, and the peg is the commandments of God and His Law in the Old Testament, to which are added in the New Testament the Holy Sacraments.

The aim of God's discipline and mercy is that we may take heed and reject sin, so that we become spiritually enlightened, see God and enjoy fellowship with Him, and spend our few days on earth, which are a preparation for heaven, where we enter into glories forever, before which all the toils of the little earth become light.

Turning away from God and falling into sin, which led to the captivity, is a time of darkness, while returning to Jerusalem and worshiping God in His temple is enlightenment, and it is the life that the people receive in the times of their worship of God in the midst of the bondage to which they are subject in Assyria, Babylon, then Media and Persia.

The mercy of God is revealed in His people through His care for them, although they were enslaved to the kings of Assyria, Babylon and Persia, so God intervenes miraculously and moves the kings of Persia, namely Cyrus and Darius, then Artaxerxes, to bring the people of God back to Jerusalem, encourage them and give them the vessels of the house of the Lord and money and timber and many gifts, that they might build the temple and worship God.

The people did not only return to Jerusalem, but built the temple in the days of Zerubbabel, then by worship in the days of Ezra, and finally God gave them a wall in Jerusalem, meaning God's protection of them, which also appeared when Nehemiah built the wall of Jerusalem and its gates.
Seek not their peace: do not make treaties of peace or alliances with them.

Ezra continues his confession on behalf of all the people, saying: What shall we say before Your many mercies, which brought us back from captivity and built the temple for us and care for us and give us all our needs? But, to our shame, before this wonderful love we disobeyed You and abandoned Your commandments, because You declared to us that the land of Canaan, which You would cause us to possess, is an unclean land through the worship of idols by those who dwell in it and all the sins connected with it, and that these sins are spread everywhere in this land.

And You commanded us not to be joined in pagan marriages, as Your prophets declared to us, such as Moses the prophet (Deut 7:1-3), and not to be joined with the pagan inhabitants of the land in treaties and alliances, indeed not to mingle with them, that we might live in our faith in the one God and in our upright conduct, and not imitate the sins of the pagans. And You promised to support us and protect us, so that we would be strong and receive the good things of the land, and even leave it as an inheritance to our children, as long as we were obedient to Your commandments.

Ezra also confesses that the divine discipline by captivity is less than what the sins of his people deserve, so he declares his confession of the abominableness of the sins that led God to punish the people with captivity. But even after He punished, His mercies appeared in bringing back the remnant of them, that is, those who love God and worship in His house, through the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, then Ezra.

Ezra denounces what his people did by returning to the breaking of God's commandments and intermarrying with pagan women. And he declares that they deserve a greater punishment, that even the remnant that returned to Jerusalem should perish, because it was defiled by the worship of idols; for rejecting God's commandments is a rejection of His person and a declaration of the people's lack of love for Him, for whoever accepts the commandment accepts God who gave it.

At the close of the prayer Ezra confesses the righteousness of God and His tenderness, which appeared in His leaving a remnant for His people, that is, those returning from captivity, whom He helped and for whom He built the temple, that they might worship Him in it.

Ezra affirmed that their sin was upon their heads, in shame and confusion before God, and he committed his life and the people to God, because they deserved every punishment because of marriage to foreign women, and he did not ask for mercy from God or help because of his sense of the shame of sin; and in confidence he left his life and his people in the hands of God, believing in His fatherhood, which would not forsake or neglect them. He felt it a great honor that God allowed him to stand and pray before Him, so he could not ask for more than this. It is a wonderful humility and an example of broken prayer and true repentance before God.

To the extent of your humility, your confession of your sins and your humbling of yourself before God, you receive many mercies, so do not let your day end before you examine yourself and confess before God, and you will receive His forgiveness and blessings.
Putting away the pagan marriages
1- The book began in the first chapter by telling us of the first return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, then the building of the temple.
2- It tells us in the seventh chapter of the return to Jerusalem under Ezra.

3- This chapter tells us of Ezra the shepherd, broken in prayer and firm in the care of his people, to cleanse them of evil by putting away the pagan marriages and all the sins connected with them, so he was able to draw the hearts of the people to himself and they obeyed him, and so they received the mercies of God.

After a contrite prayer filled with tears and humility before God, accompanied by fasting, Ezra sensed that the prayer had been answered, for those around him were moved when they heard his prayer and told others of the people. A great number of the people gathered, men, women and children, and stood behind him before the house of the Lord, praying and weeping as he did, confessing their sins and offering repentance with contrition.

Ezra resembles Moses and Paul in their intercession for their peoples before God (Ex 32:33; 2 Cor 11:29), and he is even a type of Christ, who prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane and was crucified for us, to intercede for us by His blood with an intercession of atonement that removes all our sins. That is, the supplicating intercession of Ezra, Moses and Paul is great in the eyes of God, that He may extend His mercies to us and forgive our sins in the blood of Christ.

Ezra prayed with all his heart, his garments torn and his tears pouring down, and he took no thought of his position. He was an example of deep, repentant prayer before his people, so that a huge crowd gathered and shared in his prayer and tears. It is understood from this that Ezra's prayer was long, and that during it this great people gathered, and part of this prayer was recorded in the previous chapter (ch. 9:6-15).

Shechaniah is a Hebrew word meaning "God dwells", and he was a man in whose heart God truly dwelt, and he was deeply moved by Ezra's prayer. If Jehiel his father is the one mentioned in (v. 26), then Shechaniah suffered from the problem of pagan marriages in the form of his father's pagan wife. He came forward before Ezra and the whole assembly of the people, declaring his confession of the unfaithfulness of the people, although he himself had not married a foreign woman, but he followed the example of Ezra, who confessed on behalf of his people.

A great virtue appears in Shechaniah, namely hope in God, who does not forsake His people but forgives them if they repent and obey His commandments by putting away the foreign marriages. He was not content with being moved and weeping, like the rest of the people, but came forward with a confession like Ezra's, and then with promises that we will see in the following two verses. Shechaniah here represents the people who support their leader Ezra with repentance, confession and hope, as the Church does when she prays in the Liturgy for the Pope, the bishops, the priests and the deacons.

If the unfaithfulness of one person, Achan the son of Carmi, caused defeat for all the people of God in the days of Joshua the son of Nun (Josh 7), then when unfaithfulness spreads among the people through marriage to pagan women, it requires collective repentance from the people and separation from evil, that God may have mercy and forgive.

The repentance of Shechaniah, as a representative of the people, was joined to action, so he declared the people's readiness to separate from the pagan wives and send them away with their children, that is, to cut off sin and everything connected with it; for they were the source of the evil into which they cast their husbands, in the worship of idols and all the customs of the pagans contrary to the commandments of God. This act was not cruelty on the part of Shechaniah, because the causes of evil, namely the pagan wives, must be removed; besides, if these wives loved their husbands, they had come to believe in God and worship Him and had circumcised their male children, and therefore they would not be exposed to being sent away. Especially since these marriages were not lawful and did not need a divorce, but were relationships of adultery whose only cause was lust, as is proved by his saying "put away all the wives" and not "the wives", for no marriage contract had been made for them, and therefore they did not need a bill of divorce. We see Shechaniah's submission to the Law in his saying "according to the law", and his humility in his saying "according to the counsel of my lord", that is, Ezra.

Here Shechaniah affirms the support of the people, who fear God, for Ezra, and he asks him, with the help of God, to cleanse the people of the pagan women, for God loves him and for his sake His people will see them.
Shechaniah asked Ezra to carry out the will of God by saying "for this matter belongeth unto thee", that is, carry out the Law of God to separate the people from evil.

Shechaniah was convinced of the gravity of marrying pagan women, but it was not within his authority to separate the people from them, so he looked to Ezra, who had the authority, and encouraged him to carry out the Law of God. Shechaniah was not content with weeping behind Ezra, like the rest of the people, but confessed the sin of the people and encouraged Ezra. For the people need a leader to lead them in the way of God, and the leader also needs the encouragement and support of the people. We see this in the rite of the Church in the Liturgy, how the people pray for the Pope and the bishops, that is, the spiritual leaders.

Ezra was indeed encouraged by the words of Shechaniah, so he arose and called the chief priests and the Levites and made them swear, they and all the people standing behind them, to carry out the Law of God by each one separating from his pagan wife and the children born of her, and they all agreed and swore to carry out the Law of God. Ezra took care that the decision to put away the pagan marriages should be a collective decision, so that all would be responsible for carrying it out, and thus he would ensure precision in the execution. He took special care over those responsible for the religious life of the people, the priests and the Levites, because they were the ones who would carry out this Law of God.

Ezra had been fasting all day, praying and weeping. After the people and their religious leaders agreed to put away the pagan marriages, Ezra arose and entered one of the chambers attached to the Temple, which was the room of a person called Johanan the son of Eliashib, who may have been one of the chief priests, or a priest, and there he completed his prayers, for he was not content with the agreement of the people to obey the Law. But he prayed that the carrying out of this Law might be completed, and afterward he ate food and rested, and most likely spent the night there, as one of the translations of the Bible states. Ezra represents the spiritual leader who does not cease from prayer and weeping before God for his people because of their faults, until these faults are completely removed; for it is mentioned that he mourned because of the unfaithfulness of those of the captivity.

The chief priests sent out a proclamation in every place where the tribe of Judah and those returning with it from the tribes of Israel lived, that they should come within three days to Jerusalem before the temple of God.

Although Ezra had authority to command the gathering of the people, since the king had given him this authority (ch. 7:26), he had the chief priests gather the people, so that the people would feel that the decision was from the whole community and not from one individual, and no one would try to resist the proclamation.
The proclamation was bound to a penalty for whoever did not come to Jerusalem, and this penalty was:

1- That all the property of this offender be forfeited, that is, his land and possessions be taken, which he would squander and give to his pagan wife, although they were the inheritance of God for His people.

2- He would be separated, that is, excluded and cut off from the people of God, because he was against the Law of God, so that he would feel that he was defying God, and so fear and obey the proclamation. Separation means being deprived of all the promises of God.
The proclamation gave a delay of three days, because it was a sufficient period for anyone, however far from Jerusalem he lived, to come and appear before the temple of God.

The number three signifies the Resurrection of Christ, for within this period all come to the temple of God, to declare and separate themselves from evil, so that they may rise from their lusts and live in purity before God.

Your pouring yourself out before God in fervent prayer solves all your problems, however intractable they may seem. Hold fast to prayer and be persistent with God until He restores your peace and delivers you from all evil.

entries.section: (2) The promise to leave the pagan wives

paragraphs.text: The people obeyed the chief priests and came within the three days to Jerusalem, namely the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, since they were the majority, and with them of course all those returning from the captivity from the other tribes. They gathered in a square beside the Temple, most likely the square beside the Water Gate, where the people later gathered in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 8:1). The time of their gathering was in the ninth month, that is, the month of Kislev, which corresponds to the month of December, on the twentieth day of it, and this month has abundant rains, so when they gathered in the square the rain fell heavily.

The people were afraid of God because of their sin, which exposed them to the divine wrath, and because they were about to leave their pagan wives and their children by them. All this made them tremble, in addition to their shivering from the cold of the weather and the falling of the rain, so it was a fearful assembly before God, as they awaited God's judgment upon them at the hand of His priests.

We see the response of the priests and the people to the Law of God in their immediate carrying out of the words of Ezra, after they had sworn before him to carry out the Law, and they did not postpone the proclamation because of the unsuitable weather. The people obeyed and came in the midst of the rain, because of their fear of God, who is able to destroy them on account of their sin of marrying pagan women.
The people felt that heaven was expressing the wrath of God by sending down the rain, and this increased their fear and established the spirit of repentance within them.
